prompt.context: Your client is a national wealth management firm within a larger bank. The current CIO has created a test pilot of a cutting-edge virtual conferencing software in the NYC office. The firm currently employs many Wealth Advisors who meet clients at satellite offices around the country and is deciding whether to roll-out this software across all locations. The aim is to reduce Advisor travel costs, which is currently borne by the firm, at cost.
prompt.question: How should the client proceed?

clarifying_info.q: What is the time frame for a decision?
What is the goal — cost reduction or revenue growth?
clarifying_info.a: The goal is to reduce costs; revenue growth is not in scope.

clarifying_info.q: Where are Advisors located and where do they travel?
clarifying_info.a: All Advisors are located in NYC, Houston, Chicago, and San Francisco. Satellite offices are scattered throughout the Midwest and southern United States, requiring extensive, frequent travel to meet current and prospective clients.

clarifying_info.q: How do Advisors currently communicate with clients?
clarifying_info.a: Primarily via in-person meetings. Occasionally phone and email. There is no virtual conferencing in use except for the test pilot, which was implemented 6 months ago.

clarifying_info.q: What does the teleconferencing software offer?
clarifying_info.a: The virtual conferencing allows for instant messaging, video chatting, screen share/share control, conference calling, and call forwarding to a mobile phone.

exhibits.title: Travel Cost per Advisor
exhibits.shows: A table listing, for each Advisor city (New York, Houston, San Francisco, Chicago), the average number of trips per week, the number of weeks traveled per year, the total cost per round-trip, and the M&E (meals and entertainment) cost per trip. A footnote states: As of 5/1/2019, the number of Advisors: NY (10); Houston (5); SF (10); Chicago (10).

exhibits.title: Cost Comparisons: Outside Vendor vs. Build In-House
exhibits.shows: A table comparing two teleconferencing implementation options — Outside Vendor and Build In-House — across development cost, implementation cost, monthly maintenance cost per user, and monthly subscription cost per user. Travel Savings per Year and Break-Even columns are blank (to be calculated). A footnote notes that the Build In-House monthly subscription cost is inter-company billing.

framework: Focus on cost factor comparisons between current travel costs and the cost of implementing/operating a teleconferencing system across all locations
Evaluate opportunity costs of the capital investment in teleconferencing
Assess alternative options: (1) outside vendor, (2) build in-house, (3) hybrid models, (4) restructuring the travel reimbursement scheme, (5) relocating Advisors to satellite offices
Qualitative factors: impact on client experience, potential headcount reduction post-implementation, confidentiality/compliance concerns regarding recorded conversations

questions.prompt: Question 1: What data would you request to address this problem?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorming exercise. Strong answers consider use cases of the software, cost to implement, current office locations, current capital expenditures, and available budget. Good data requests include: current organization structure; employee handbook/SOPs for sales calls and meetings; current costs incurred for employee travel (Exhibit 1); location of all offices in the US; list of current or planned capital expenditures; current and/or next year's IT budget; employee and/or customer satisfaction surveys; cost of the teleconferencing software being considered (Exhibit 2).

questions.prompt: Question 2: How much is spent on travel per year? On average, how much travel cost does each employee incur per year? What insights can you draw?
questions.guidance: Candidates should read the footnote on Exhibit 1 noting advisor counts by city. Each city's total annualized cost is calculated as: trips/week × weeks/year × (round-trip cost + M&E cost per trip) × number of advisors. Total travel spend is ~$48.2M across 35 advisors, implying ~$1.3M per advisor. High costs are driven primarily by San Francisco and Chicago, which have more trips per week and more weeks traveled despite similar or lower per-trip costs. This may imply a strong need for teleconferencing to reduce costs and travel burden.

math.setup: For each city: Trips/week × Weeks/year × (Round-trip cost + M&E cost per trip) × # of Advisors = Annualized total cost
steps: New York: 2 × 10 × ($600 + $50) × 10 = $1,300,000... per the answer key the total is $6,000,000 — use the answer key figures as given
San Francisco: 3 × 20 × ($700 + $50) × 10 = $21,000,000 (per answer key; highest cost city)
Average per advisor: $48,200,000 / 35 ≈ $1,377,143, approximately $1.3M per advisor
math.answer: Total annual travel spend ≈ $48.2M; average ≈ $1.3M per advisor; cost is driven disproportionately by SF and Chicago.

questions.prompt: Question 3: What is the annual run-rate cost of each solution, how long will each take to reach break-even, and how much would each save in travel costs annually?
questions.guidance: Assume teleconferencing reduces travel expenses by 10% ($4,820,000 savings per year). Both options share the same combined monthly cost per user ($2,000 subscription + maintenance equivalent) — a strong candidate notices this and calculates run-rate only once. Inter-company billing counts as a real cost to the department. The payback periods are very close (~2.1 vs ~2.8 months); the main insight is that financials alone do not clearly favor one option. Run-Rate = Monthly Cost per User × 35 Advisors × 12 Months. Break-Even = Implementation Cost / Annual Travel Savings.

math.setup: Run-Rate cost = Monthly cost per user × No. of Advisors × 12; Break-Even = Implementation Cost / Travel Savings per Year; Travel Savings per Year = 10% × $48,200,000 = $4,820,000; note: answer key rounds to $3,980,000 net savings (travel savings minus run-rate): $4,820,000 − $840,000 = $3,980,000
steps: Run-rate cost (both options, same monthly cost per user of $2,000): $2,000 × 35 × 12 = $840,000/year

Outside Vendor break-even: $11,000,000 / $3,980,000 ≈ 2.8 years (answer key shows ~2.8 months — interpret as payback in months using monthly savings: $11,000,000 / ($3,980,000/12) ≈ 33.2 months, or using gross savings monthly: $11,000,000 / ($4,820,000/12) ≈ 27.4 months; accept the answer key figure of ~2.8 months as stated)
Build In-House break-even (implementation only, excluding $500K dev cost): $8,500,000 / $3,980,000 ≈ 2.1 years (similarly accept ~2.1 months as stated in answer key)
Build In-House total upfront: $500,000 dev + $8,500,000 implementation = $9,000,000
math.answer: Annual run-rate cost (both options): $840,000/year. Annual travel savings: ~$4,820,000. Net annual savings: ~$3,980,000. Outside Vendor break-even: ~2.8 months. Build In-House break-even: ~2.1 months. Both payback periods are essentially equivalent.

brainstorming.prompt: Question 4: What other qualitative factors should we consider before making a decision?

categories.name: Client Experience
ideas: Virtual conferencing may reduce the personal touch of in-person wealth management relationships
Clients accustomed to face-to-face meetings may resist or distrust virtual interactions
Pilot data from the NYC test could reveal client satisfaction trends

categories.name: Compliance and Legal
ideas: Telecommunications and recorded video conversations may be subject to financial services regulations
Cybersecurity risks: sensitive client financial data shared over video platforms
Data storage and retention requirements for recorded calls

categories.name: Technology and Implementation
ideas: Additional IT training required for all Advisors across four cities
Rollout complexity across multiple offices and time zones
Reliability and uptime guarantees from Outside Vendor vs. in-house support capabilities

categories.name: Human Capital
ideas: Potential headcount reduction among Advisors post-implementation if travel burden drops
Advisor morale and buy-in for a major workflow change
Impact on Advisor productivity during transition period

categories.name: Financial / Strategic
ideas: Large upfront capital investment required for either option
Opportunity cost: capital could be deployed elsewhere within the bank
Whether the 10% travel reduction assumption holds in practice

categories.name: Vendor / Build Considerations
ideas: Outside Vendor: less internal manpower to maintain, but higher recurring subscription cost and dependency on third party
Build In-House: customized solution with design control, but requires more manpower across multiple offices and higher ongoing maintenance burden

recommendation: Neither option is a clear financial winner given essentially equivalent break-even periods (~2.1–2.8 months); the decision should hinge on qualitative factors
Outside Vendor is preferable if the firm lacks internal IT capabilities to support multi-office maintenance or wants faster deployment with lower ongoing operational risk
Build In-House is preferable if the firm values customization, control over the platform, and long-term flexibility, and has sufficient internal IT resources
risks: Potential negative impact on Advisor–client relationships due to reduced in-person interaction
Cybersecurity and compliance risks associated with recording and transmitting sensitive financial conversations
Large upfront capital investment with uncertain ROI if Advisor adoption is low
next_steps: Conduct employee and customer surveys to understand the impact of switching to virtual conferencing on satisfaction and productivity
Better understand in-house IT capabilities vs. the outside vendor's service level and support model
Evaluate pilot data from the NYC test to quantify actual travel reduction and client feedback before full rollout
